\begin{bankq}[id=SI12-P2-PHY-S2-Q01, source={Score-I - Test 12 (09 Mar 2022)}, paper=2, qno=1, type=numerical, subtopic={Surface tension}, answer={1.50}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S3 I1 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: surface tension force on a soap film, equilibrium | steps: geometry of the film between the squares; vertical component of tension per side; total upward force; weight of the small square; solve for h | I: the film tilts so only a component supports the weight}]
Figure shows a soap film formed between two square figures made of a uniform wire. The bigger square is held while keeping it in a horizontal plane and the smaller square is slowly allowed to drop vertically. It reaches an equilibrium state after dropping a height $h$. Let surface tension of soap $=T$. Mass per unit length of wire $=\lambda$. Acceleration due to gravity $=g$. Given that $h=\dfrac{n\lambda ga}{\sqrt{4T^2-\lambda^2g^2}}$; find the value $n$.
\bfig{158.2}{SI12_p2_phy_s2_q01_1.png}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI12-P2-PHY-S2-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 12 (09 Mar 2022)}, paper=2, qno=2, type=numerical, subtopic={Viscosity}, answer={2.00}, answer_src=key, difficulty=2, diff_parts={K1 S1 I0 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: terminal velocity in a viscous fluid | steps: mg = buoyancy + 6 pi eta r v, with rho = 2 rho\_L gives v = 2 cm/s}]
A spherical ball of density $\rho$ and radius 0.003 m is dropped into a tube containing a viscous fluid. Viscosity of the fluid $=1.260$ N.m$^{-2}$ and its density $\rho_L=\rho/2=1260$ kg.m$^{-3}$. Find its terminal speed in cm/s. ($g=$ acceleration due to gravity $=10$ ms$^{-2}$)
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SII18-P1-PHY-S2-Q07, source={Score-II - Test 18 (13 Feb 2024)}, paper=1, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={Surface tension}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: standard problem in this chapter, surface tension, apply the relevant results | steps: apply the relevant results; compute}]
A drop of liquid of volume V is squeezed between two parallel smooth plates unit the liquid thickness h is very small compared with the liquid's radial extent R. The liquid/plate/air contact angle $\alpha$, and the liquid/air surface tension is $\sigma$. Gravitational effects are negligible.

\begin{center}
\bfigi{233.8}{SII18_p1phy_q7_liquid.png}
\end{center}

\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{If $\alpha\simeq0$, then pressure inside liquid will be lesser by $\left(\dfrac{2\sigma}{h}\right)$ as compared to P$_{atm}$.}
\opt{B}{If $\alpha\simeq0$, then pressure inside liquid will be more by $\left(\dfrac{2\sigma}{h}\right)$ compared to P$_{atm}$.}
\opt{C}{If upper plate is massless then upward force required to hold the plate in equilibrium will be approximately $\sigma 2\pi R\sin\alpha + \left(\dfrac{2\sigma}{h}\right)\pi R^2\ (0<\alpha<90)$}
\opt{D}{If upper plate is massless then upward force required to hold the plate in equilibrium will be approximately $\sigma 2\pi R\sin\alpha - \left(\dfrac{2\sigma}{h}\right)\pi R^2\ (0<\alpha<90)$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SA01-P1-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score Advanced - Test 01 (22 Sep 2020)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=single, subtopic={Pressure}, answer={A}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: hemisphere filled through a tube, pressure | steps: pressure of the liquid; force on the hemisphere; condition for lifting}]

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SRGBT07-P1-PHY-S1-G15-16, source={SRGBT - Test 07 (05 Sep 2021)}, questions={15-16}]
The fact that the density of ice is smaller than the density of water has an important consequence for homeowners, who have to contend with the possibility of bursting water pipes during severe winters. Water often freezes in a section of pipe exposed to unusually cold temperatures. The ice can form an immovable plug that prevents the subsequent flow of water, as Figure illustrates. When water (larger density) turns to ice (smaller density), its volume expands by 10\%. When ice forms on the right side of the plug, the expanding ice pushes liquid to the right. But it has nowhere to go if the faucet is closed. As ice continues to form and expand, the water pressure between the plug and faucet rises. The bulk modulus of ice is much more than that of the water. So water gets compressed. Even a small increase in the amount of ice produces a large increase in the pressure. Therefore, the pipe can burst at any point where it is structurally weak. There is a simple way to prevent pipes from bursting. Simply open the faucet, so it drips a little. The excessive pressure will be relieved.\par
\bfig{137.4}{SRGBT07_p1_phy_s0_q14_2.png}
\end{bankpassage}
